the identification of unseen fake news by acquiring robust skills to pinpoint
new patterns within limited annotated data.  It utilizes standard text
classification methods as meta learners, which consist of modules to identify
informative elements and reconstruct complex representations.  Our research
demonstrates that MetaFEND significantly surpasses conventional news detection
models on both synthetic and real datasets for the task of identifying previously
unseen fake news, achieving state-of-the-art performance.  Our MetaFEND
source code and models are accessible on GitHub.

This study considers a one-dimensional periodic transport equation, not decaying over time and featuring a nonlocal flow condition. We demonstrate that, regardless of how smooth it is, the solution will eventually become an function of just two variables when not dissipating. Specifically, for the equation not decaying over time with a nonlocal flow condition, we prove that the solution's smoothness cannot be maintained indefinitely. We show there is a particular moment in time, which can be calculated, after which the solution behaves like a function of two independent variables. This result is then applied to another similar equation, and we discover its solution will also lose its infinite smoothness at a calculable point, indicating it will be like a function of just one variable.

This research examines the feasibility of quaternary Golay complementary array (GCA) pairs consisting of four-element arrays within a quaternary system. We discover that GCAPs can only be realized in specific scenarios: when the spectral spread values match in magnitude but differ in sign, or when they are equal to zero. To validate these findings, simulation experiments were conducted and results showed significant performance gains in terms of reduced main lobe width and side lobe width compared to conventional direct sequence code division multiple access (DSSS) systems with single-user access.

Utilizing a detailed first-principles method, we calculated how dopants should be positioned within a silicon crystal to maximize the spin interaction between two electrons while maintaining electrical neutrality. We examined various configurations in different silicon structures that met the valence band filling requirement and had equivalent total energies. By examining various configurations in different silicon lattices and comparing their spin exchange strengths, we identified the optimal placement of dopants to maximize the spin exchange interaction while keeping the system electrically neutral and at the same total energy. In the case of n-type silicon, we found that the most effective spin exchange interaction between two electrons occurs when both are placed in adjacent atomic sites on an antiprismatic plane with the dopants in interstitial positions. This interaction is estimated at approximately 170 Kelvin for nitrogen-bored silicon and may be even stronger in other n-type settings. Notably, this is substantially higher than previously reported values in literature and suggests that surface states found in thin-film or nanowire structures could potentially host a quintuple with a spin exchange interaction as high as 5 kilokelvins.

We introduce an innovative method for building Bayesian networks without requiring labeled data for new instances. By leveraging only unlabelled unstructured time series observations, our model learns to identify the structure and parameters of a new instance using only a few inference examples. Our approach utilizes deep autoencoders to discover hidden variables representing the parameters of a Bayesian network, and employs time series observations to learn the prior distribution of these variables for each new instance. Evaluations using synthetic and real-world data demonstrate the effectiveness of our model in recovering the prior distribution for new instances and achieving accurate inference, using only a few examples with static properties. Our work extends previous research by eliminating the need to specify a pre-determined set of Bayesian network structures and allowing for a broader range of possibilities.

A polished version of the ROBUST construction for polynomial rings in graded rings is presented as a homogeneous construction over the category of spectra. Specifically, the connection between the polynomial rings of a finite collection of spheres and those of complex projective spaces derived from them is described using this construction. The corresponding connection between the ring of functions on these spaces can then be interpreted as a filtered structure with associated graded object equivalent to the original rings. In turn, this allows for the computation of parts of the cohomology of the complex projective spaces based on the partitions of the original spheres' cohomology degrees within the mod $p$ setting.

Deep learning-based methods have rapidly advanced in using convolutional neural networks (CNNs) for segmenting key areas within medical images.  A notable milestone was achieved in 2018 when CNNs reached a high level of accuracy in segmenting key anatomical structures within 3D heart MRI scans, matching the state-of-the-art standards.  This breakthrough was made possible by a substantial increase in training datasets and innovative CNN designs that utilized internal knowledge and attention mechanisms.  This paper provides a comprehensive review of the recent advancements in CNN-based methods for anatomical segmentation, detailing the step-by-step progression of CNN models, large-scale strategies for anatomical segmentation, and advances in multi-modal and multi-organ segmentation.  By focusing on key milestones and design innovations, this review aims to provide readers with a clear understanding of the evolution of state-of-the-art CNN-based segmentation models and the associated strategies for anatomical segmentation.

GP 2 is an evolution of GP, which is a graph-based programming language that
utilizes a specific data structure to represent graph edges and graph programs,
which take advantage of this data structure's performance benefits. GP 2 expands
upon GP by introducing new graph transformations whose left-hand sides are defined
using the same data structure. In GP 2's performance evaluation, which mirrors GP's methodology,
the transformation of graphs by programs experiences less slowdown when applying
rights-hand sides. Initially, a library was created to define the data structure
on the left-hand side and transform it accordingly. Yet GP 2's performance metrics
revealed suboptimal results when comparing before and after transformation times.
Further analysis of graph programs led to a major update of the data structure and
the compiler, which significantly reduced processing times for programs after transformation.

In the proposed framework, we decompose either unsupervised or supervised feature extraction into simpler components using representational learning, which can be achieved through a variety of methods. For unsupervised learning, we demonstrate how to construct a robust and simple framework that creates a robust feature set, capable of generalizing to new data. Our approach yields state-of-the-art results on multiple datasets for both unsupervised and supervised scenarios. Similarly, we discuss the application of representational learning to construct features that work effectively for both unsupervised and supervised tasks.

We present several infinite families of graphs with unbounded twin-automorphism groups, which mirror key properties of a specific family of "twin-reachable" graphs previously discovered by A. A. Assis in 2019. These new families are denoted as $\mathcal{G}_1, \mathcal{G}_2$, and $\mathcal{G}_3$. Each family is defined as follows: $\mathcal{G}_1$ consists of graphs with a comparable or smaller automorphism group relative to a "twin-reachable" family, $\mathcal{G}_2$ comprises graphs with the same vertex set size as the "twin-reachable" family, and $\mathcal{3}$ consists of graphs with a significantly larger vertex set compared to the "twin-reachable" family. Verifying that each family exists and has unbounded automorphism groups can be efficiently achieved using computer assistance. However, to formally prove their characteristics, manual calculations are necessary. Each of these families is defined by a set of basic components arranged in a specific pattern, and individual graphs within each family can be constructed with a quadratic number of vertices, edges, and automorphisms in relation to this parameter. A direct consequence is that specific instances within each of these families are computationally irreducible.

A class of regularization techniques, including Group Lasso, enables efficient selection of variables by constraining model complexity. We define and analyze a new method, the Vexing Group Lasso, applicable to both continuous and categorical data types. This alternative formulation of the penalty term in the Vexing Group Lasso results in the general form of the model coefficients being sparse, leading to enhanced model interpretability and reduced model dimensionality. A gradient-based optimization algorithm, with modifications to ensure model sparsity at each step, is proposed for the development of the Vexing Group Lasso. Numerical experiments demonstrate the Vexing Group Lasso's ability to produce accurate and interpretable models across a range of synthetic data sets.

Recent advances in natural language processing include the release of several datasets containing lists of statements composed of natural language sentences that contain named entities and relations, which are directly linked to Knowledge Graphs (KGs). This study investigates the effectiveness of models pre-trained on KG-based data for the task of semantic parsing, specifically for the entity resolution task. Our evaluation reveals state-of-the-art performance for a baseline model using an T5 variant, achieving a score of 71.5 on the SParQ entity parsing test set. Our findings also highlight the importance of data consisting of statements composed of natural language that are anchored to Knowledge Graphs for the task of semantic parsing. A model featuring a KG-based curriculum pre-training strategy outperforms models pre-trained on KG triples and data augmented with Wikipedia. Additionally, our study provides insights into model attention patterns related to entity mentions within parsed statements.

This paper introduces a novel line drawing algorithm that lines
utilizes multiplicative matrix operations to lines of different shapes,
particularly effective in rendering fan-shaped line joins. The proposed
method mitigates performance issues associated with fan-shaped lines by
reducing the rendering workload, achieved by omitting data for lines
situated outside a specific angular range. The algorithm is
unsuccessful with rounded line joins due to the intricate geometry of
data within a certain range. Performance assessments demonstrate
enhanced rendering efficiency for line joins in the adjacent range
when utilizing multiplicative matrix operations, whereas additive
matrix operations offer reduced performance gains. Furthermore,
performance advantages of the proposed method are evident in scenes
populated by numerous line segments, particularly when line styles
with data within the rejected range are absent, thus avoiding
multiplicative matrix operations. However, performance gains of the
proposed method are curtailed when line styles with data within the
specific range are rendering.

To improve speech enhancement within the time-frequency domain, a novel model called the Dual-Path Convolution Recurrent Network (DPCRN) has been proposed. This model combines two distinct paths: one utilizing convolutional networks to capture short-term patterns of prior enhancement estimates, and another utilizing convolutional convolution networks to analyze the short-term patterns of raw noisy input signals. The network then integrates these short-term patterns with long-term patterns derived from the enhancement estimates through Convolutional Recurrent Networks (CRNs). Notably, the DPCRN architecture is designed to be fully plug-and-play with existing time-frequency masking methods. Extensive experiments conducted with two public datasets demonstrate the superior performance of DPCRN compared to state-of-the-art plug-and-play based speech enhancement methods.

We present simple two-fluid model for two-dimensional Rayleigh-B\'enard convection that effectively captures a key characteristic of this phenomenon's non-equilibrium dynamics.  Our model comprises an entropic fluid responsible for transporting heat and a cooler, non-entropic fluid with uniform temperature.  Based on the principles of this model, we made several predictions regarding the system's heat flux behavior under varying conditions, specifically, $\langle Bz^{-1}\rangle\sim\Ra^{1/2}$ in a setting without thermal boundary layer resistance and $\langle Bz^{-2}\rangle\sim\Ra^{2/3}$ in a setting with thermal boundary layer resistance, where $B$ denotes the Nusselt number and $\Ra$ denotes the Rayleigh number.

We examine the creation of entanglement between two initially independent atoms interacting with a cavity whose entanglement levels with each atom may vary. By leveraging the collective spin of the atoms, we investigate the production of Multipartite Entanglement in scenarios where the cavity is either continuously interacting with the atoms or discretely tied to one of them. Under specific conditions, the system can achieve significant entanglement without requiring prior knowledge of the atoms' individual states. Notably, the inability of the atoms to communicate with each other, resulting from their isolated interaction with the cavity, actually enhances the capacity for generating multipartite entanglement when the cavity is prepared in a state that does not exhibit correlations, as well as in more intricate scenarios. Furthermore, the potential for creating entanglement across all initial states of the atoms is demonstrated, and the resulting collective state can be achieved through measurements that do not rely on knowing the atoms' prior states.

Social media sentiment analysis has become crucial in understanding public opinion,  particularly through sentiment classification in tweets. This task's complexity arises from the need to process large amounts of data and handle various challenges, such as spelling mistakes and ambiguous language. Recent studies have focused on developing robust classification models by leveraging extensive datasets and technical techniques like LSTM. This study builds upon previous work by evaluating an LSTM-based sentiment classification model from the GitHub repository on the GDEA2019 dataset consisting of English tweets. The results show that the LSTM model achieved high accuracy rates, with macro F1-scores reaching 84.9% and 90.5% in different classification settings. This study's findings contribute to advancing social media sentiment analysis by evaluating and enhancing existing models and provide a valuable resource for future researchers in the field.

Utilizing the non-linear Yang-Mills charge as a critical parameter, a non-Abelian gauge theory was employed to examine the evolution of black hole dynamics and thermodynamics in four-dimensional spacetime. As the theory's non-linearity increases, both the shadow cast by a black hole and its thermal radiation become broader and broader-spectrums, particularly within a specific range of frequencies. Furthermore, there is a direct correlation between a black hole's mass and its thermal profile, which becomes broader with increasing non-linearity of the theory. It is also observed that the threshold frequency above which a black hole does not radiate any more energy, is inversely proportional to its non-linearity. As the non-Abelian charge grows, both larger and hotter areas of a black hole's shadow become concentrated in its central region, while its peripheral areas expand at higher frequencies. Ultimately, there is an optimal non-linear Yang-Mills charge that maximizes a black hole's temperature and thermal radiation, after which the radiation starts to decline and the mass of hot black holes becomes more uniform.

A new method is proposed for analyzing optical tomograms based on the spectral representation of the Weygand-Wigner transform, which allows for the identification and quantification of classical and nonclassical features within quantum states of light. When optical tomograms are viewed as comprising a spectrum of elementary components, each corresponding to the distribution of a specific angular momentum state, both the classical and nonclassical characteristics of the state become apparent in the form of presence or absence, and weight in the component spectrum. The underlying theory is demonstrated through the analysis of the quantum states of the photon polarization.

Viewers of high-definition videos such as VR and $360$-degree videos often encounter a limited viewport, restricting their view to a small portion of the entire video content. To enhance streaming performance and reduce data loading times, accurate viewport prediction is crucial for prioritizing video segments within the viewports. While previous studies have produced promising results, they neglect an important clue present in many immersive videos: video subtitles. In this paper, a Subtitle-Based Viewport Prediction (SBVP) approach is proposed to leverage this information present in video subtitres, which are frequently encountered in such videos. Given that subtitres are typically static and confined to a specific region of the video viewports, SBVP enhances the accuracy of viewports prediction by analyzing subtitle distribution. Experimental results using a real-world dataset demonstrate SBVP's significant improvement in viewports prediction accuracy, particularly when subtitles are present, thus validating the value of presentational data for viewports prediction.

To calculate thermal states and thermal evolution using the density matrix renormalization group (DMRG) method, we must employ a thermal PEPO (parallelized environment projected operator) state that maintains a bond dimension independent of the system's size. This achievement is made possible by leveraging the symmetries of a Hamiltonian to construct PEPOs with constant bond dimensions. Our approach utilizes these symmetries to approximate thermal states and evolve systems with quadratic DMRG (t-DMRG) efficiency, opening up possibilities to study thermal phenomena in models where symmetries constrain high-bond requirement conditions. This includes investigating the thermalization of models with large constant bond dimension requirements relative to their traditional definitions.

We reconstruct decoupling surfaces for a pair of coupled master equations with Poissonian noise using a two-step method. Firstly, we apply Taylor series analysis to identify the order and approximate location of surfaces where significant changes occur. Then, we reverse the process to determine the intrinsic curvature of these surfaces and classify them canonically. As an illustration, we examine the coherent decoupling of the mean photon and atom numbers in a driven, dissipated two-level system.

This letter presents a comprehensive analysis of the impact of renormalons in the global fit of gluon distribution functions, focusing on the momentum sum rule. A model for these renormalons is incorporated into a phenomenological model of the gluon, which is then integrated into a standard parton distribution fitting procedure alongside the model's uncertainty estimation. Our findings show that the infrared renormalons contribute approximately 20% to the overall uncertainty of the gluon parameterization.

We investigated the influence of a magnetic field on the optical properties 
of a surface plasmon polaritons magnetophotonic crystal surface, where the 
Crystal consists of an alternating pattern of gold strips and a 
 aluminium film.  When a current passes through this structure, a 
 interaction between the surface plasmons and the Rayleigh anomaly occurs, 
 which is significantly affected by applying a perpendicular magnetic field 
 that alters key elements of the spectral pattern, including the anomalous 
 edge of the Rayleigh anomaly and the coupled states of the anomaly.  Using 
 Drude models, Fourier transformations and Dyson equations, we constructed 
 spectral representations and calculated optical conductivity to analyze these 
 phenomena.  Our research provides the necessary framework for further 
 investigations into surface structures and photonic applications that 
 leverage the Anomalous Rayleigh effect.

This paper presents a novel decision-based black-box knowledge distillation model, DB3, which significantly differs from decision-based distillation approaches (D3) by deriving training knowledge from white-box models and student model decisions rather than the teacher. Unlike the original, DB3 incorporates sample selection, curvature-aware loss functions, and curvature estimation to enhance the effectiveness of the method. Experimental results show that without any knowledge, B3's model outperforms the baseline on student accuracy by 10 percent with a limited white-box model. Additionally, DB3's model shows a 20 percent boost in accuracy when using curved loss functions and sample selection under the same constraints.

Researchers measured several branching fractions for charm mesons decaying into light hadrons, including $D^0 \rightarrow \pi^+\pi^0$, $K^+\pi^-\pi^0$, and $K_S^0\pi^+\pi^0$, as well as $H_c^+ \rightarrow \pi^-\pi^+\pi^+\pi^0$. The results for these decays are consistent with previous findings, with uncertainties primarily stemming from knowledge of production cross-sections and reconstruction efficiencies.

Let $K$ be a field of characteristic not equal to $2$. Given a multiplicity-free module $L$ over a quiver $Q$, we can compose the identity map of $Q$ with a lattice reconstruction of the submodule lattice of $Q$ in order to obtain a representation of the resulting quiver. We demonstrate that this process yields the original quiver if and only if, for each component in the decomposition of $L$ into its irreducible parts, its corresponding lattice has a one-to-one mapping of submodule lattices.

Imitation learning methods, including those based on demonstration analysis, have been highly successful in various multi-agent tasks. However, learning without requiring examples from experts has been proved less effective due to the vast amount of data necessary to cover the state-action space. Imitation learning using examples has been used in many applications, but the requirement to obtain demonstrations from experts limits its scalability significantly. Co-imitation learning was introduced to solve this challenge by leveraging the collaboration between agents, allowing them to learn from each other's actions rather than those from experts. As a result, the agents only need to share recorded trajectories, which can be processed automatically. Our Co-imitation learning framework was successfully applied to the multi-agent version of StarCraft II, known as AUV5, where we showed that it is possible to learn high-performing policies even with a small amount of examples and a limited state space resolution. Furthermore, we found that co-imitation learning outperformed traditional methods on the single-agent and multi-agent settings, as shown by nearly 10% more successful tasks completed in simulated evaluations.

We examine an algorithm used in sequential decoding, which functions independently of the decoding algorithm's type, evaluating the difference in the Hamming distance between the received sequence and sequences that are potential versions of the transmitted quasi-bernoulli sequence, of which there are typically very few. A key aspect of this method is how we define the threshold that determines the Hamming distance threshold, of which we explore several options, of which we use the polarized cutoff rate as one, to which we assess its performance. Our examination involves extensive simulations of a Tesla decoder for a wide range of block lengths, code rates and channel conditions, comparing our cutoff rates and evaluating their performance. Our simulations show that when the block length is at least 1024 and either the code rate is not extremely low or the channel is not very poor, using the polarized cutoff rate as our threshold results in a noticeable decrease in the number of Hamming distance calculations required to achieve a desired error probability compared to other cutoff rates we have examined.

Reinforcement learning (RL) has been used in automatic translation to obtain significant gains, particularly from the concept of assisted editing. In this approach, a professional editor modifies the translated text and a small agent is then employed to make fine-tuned modifications with the aim of minimizing a discrepancy between the final output and a reference. Although it is argued that this method can deliver substantial improvements, it is limiting as it is necessary to provide a corresponding target that mirrors the actual data, which is rarely feasible in real-world applications. In response to this challenge, we propose an innovative idea of optimizing the action space of the RL model, which is referred to as Space-Expanded Assisted Editing (SEE). By selectively providing a discrepancy signal based on the presence of content vs. surface form errors in the reference, we can expand the action space and achieve significant performance gains. The SEE framework can effectively utilize assisted editing in machine translation without the need for feasible conditions, which we confirm through several experiments.

A fundamental question in the theory of open systems is under what conditions can the direction of information flow between the system and its surroundings be reversed. We provide a practical, measurable way to evaluate systems that exchange information with their environment and demonstrate their bidirectional capabilities using a spin system and its surroundings. In our finding that the system's environment can exchange information, we derive an index to quantify the direction of information flow. In order to do this, we create a novel experimental setup in which the measurements are conducted that distinguish between correlations which contain anti-correlations and those that do not. It is finally shown that our indicator correctly predicts the point at which quantum bidirectionality can emerge.

We investigate biharmonic hypersurfaces within Euclidean space that exhibit a specific property, known as $\mathfrak{R}$-minimal, which encompasses minimal hypersurfaces. In this context, we identify an issue with a result from the literature, then proceed to establish corrected results and explore the characteristics of such surfaces in Euclidean and Minkowskian spaces. However, we face the obstacle of an unrecurrent operator posing a condition for a surface to be considered minimal.

This article investigates $p/q$-recognisable sets, particularly examining their properties, whether they can be represented in a specific format, and providing proofs for these representations. It focuses on characterising $p/q$-recognisable subsets of Euclidean space $(p/q)^d$ for any positive integer $d$, particularly demonstrating their 1-recognisability when $p$ and $q$ are coprime. It also proves the set defined by inequalities involving the function $
u_p/q$ has $p/q$-recognisability, further illustrating this with the set $\{(x,y)\in(N_p/q)^2\mid 
u_p/q(x)\leqslant y\leqslant 
u_p/q(x)+1\}$ has $p/q$-recognisability.

TheWIREDTIGER, REPLICASET, and SHARDEDCLUSTER configurations in the latest MongoDB releases demonstrate strong compatibility with two prominent snapshot isolation standards known as VC-Snapshot-Isolation and HS-Snapshot-Isolation, respectively. This research result was achieved through careful examination of the MongoDB source code and extensive empirical testing. Verification was initially conducted manually by analyzing the return values of critical functions in the MongoDB source code, and then confirmed automatically using a custom tool called mongobev, written in BEV language. This tool's output served as evidence for theWIREDTIGER, REPLICASET, and SHARDEDCLUSTER variants of snapshot isolation.

This research further applies the $\e$ variable to various objects, including the
sum of certain monomials from Dyck paths with two rises and semistandard tableaux
with two rows, thus providing a revised understanding of these functions when set
to a specific value. Through this approach, the research leverages existing
combinatorial interpretations of the small $\e$ parameter to establish its
properties, specifically $\e$-positivity of the function $s_2(\omega X^\e)$ and
the expansion of $s_{11}(\e)$ in terms of power sums. Consequently, the
results offer a combinatorial explanation of the $\e$-expansion of $s_{11}(\e)$
based on Dyck paths, as well as an alternative, combinatorial interpretation of
the small $\e$ parameter in the fundamental representation case.

We investigate the Ising model within a triangular network that fully accounts for the varied triangle configurations present in real-world structures. Our findings demonstrate that the complex geometry of networks gives rise to hysteresis loops with distinct characteristics, heavily influenced by specific features, and can even result in loops with open ends. Our results highlight the significance of precise triangular network models for modeling systems with magnetic hysteresis properties.

We employed the SOAR and Vatican Radio Observatory facilities, along with data from the STIX instrument on the Solar Dynamics Observatory satellite and the eIT instrument on the Solar Telescope Network, to examine three major solar flares occurring in 2018 at heliocentric distances of 0.71 and 1.0 AU. These flares were observed in X-ray, UV, and visible light spectra. Detailed study of their spectra enabled us to determine the energies necessary for different types of solar particles to escape the Sun's gravitational pull. Our analysis revealed that the distributions of these energies are similar at small heliocentric distances and at 1 AU, allowing us to refine our understanding of how solar particle energies behave over distance. Furthermore, we found that all-flare average profiles in both X-ray and UV light provide estimation tools for future solar particle events.

This paper presents a proposed model based on transfer learning and fine-tuning techniques to examine its adaptability in the domain of emotion recognition. In order to achieve this, we developed a simple yet effective model that can be easily applied to various scenarios. Our research utilizes the NLPCC2018 dataset for initial training and the SemEmNLP2020 dataset for fine-tuning. To further validate our findings, we employed additional datasets including SemEm1.0 and SemEm2.0. To facilitate future research, we released the model's weights for the BERT-base Chinese emotion recognition task on the MSRA Emotion dataset. Our results show that the proposed transfer learning and fine-tuning approach yields substantial improvements over baseline models. Specifically, we observed an accuracy gain of 4.7% on the test set using the NLPCC2018 dataset. Moreover, our research highlights that the proposed model exhibits significant flexibility in recognizing emotions across different datasets and languages.

In strong shocks with a sufficiently high adiabatic exponent, a phenomenon known as reverse-Shu structure can occur, particularly in situations where sediment is present.  This situation is highly relevant to observations made by recent missions such as Grail, which have detected gravitational anomalies in lunar crater impact regions.  To examine these events, we used a one-dimensional, unsteady shock hydrodynamics model and found that a reverse-Shu structure forms automatically as part of the shock's structure.  By applying this model to impacts on the Moon, we found that small to medium-sized impacts create a compressed sedimentary ring around the shock wave, while larger impacts create a metallic ring.  These structures may be detected using future high-resolution gravitational missions on the Moon.

Preclusive hadron decays, such as B to D plus pi, have theoretically complex structures that result in multiple form factors and separation scales. This makes caprini-lellouch-neubert and boyd-grinstein-lebed frameworks differ in their approach to scaling and parametrizing decay rates. This study offers an integrated view on these frameworks, showing their shared aspects as well as the connections between different form factors, and discusses the interface with the hadrons' composite nature from the perspective of light-cone sum rules.

Researchers have examined specific 1D SUSY quantum potentials that maintain smooth behavior under certain conditions. These potentials exhibit identical spectral characteristics to the harmonic oscillator when evaluated using polynomial versions of Heisenberg algebra. Through application of Witten's method, these potentials were successfully mapped to their deeper counterparts. Notably, the depths of these potentials align with the parameters defining the harmonic oscillator within the polynomial Heisenberg framework. Through direct solution of their Schrödinger equations, we found their characteristic energies and wave functions match those of the harmonic oscillator with varying zero-point energy levels. Through direct computation, the potentials were shown to match the harmonic oscillator, confirming our initial assumptions regarding the properties of the polynomial Heisenberg algebra.

This research introduces a novel approach to determining Lyapunov exponents in complex systems, using a model-based optimization technique that incorporates a sensitivity analysis component and a root-finding mechanism to identify the Lyapunov exponent linked to a specific system state. The validity and effectiveness of this method are demonstrated through various chaotic models and their associated datasets.

Calculations of radiative corrections to vacuum average energy and Casimir energy have also been carried out using the dimensional regularisation method. Furthermore, the modified vacuum average trace anomaly and shape anomaly have been calculated, and their combined influence has been explored.

This research paper develops an integral formula to calculate the average cost of options execution in a Cox-Iglesiases-Jarque (2009) double stochastic volatility model, which accounts for stochastic target processes and initial positions. Consequently, an inverse Laplace transform is used to calculate the distribution function of the hedging cost, which leads to an inverse Fourier transform that yields the characteristic function required to determine option prices.

Precise measurement of beam-beam closed orbit (BBCO) deviations between proton and electron beams in the Large Hadron Collider is discussed. A simple method to quantify these differences directly over the entire beam-beam interaction region has been outlined, utilizing extensive data from the BBBCO and related parameters. Notable influences on the measurements include their sensitivity to local and global orbit distortions, as well as their accuracy in determining overall and localized beam effects. Various corrections that can minimize discrepancies between the two beams and their accompanying skew quadrupole errors were examined. A significant impact of the BBCO measurements on future upgrades, notably the high-luminosity phase, including both technical requirements and design integration was also discussed.

A primary challenge in distributed optimization lies in preserving seamless
communication among non-malicious agents. In this work, we investigate robust
communication maintenance through construction of a spanning tree among
non-malicious agents, with the additional complication that the set of
non-malicious agents is unknown. We further assume that these agents must
establish connections using limited communication links. To address this
challenge, our proposed method involves encoding a spanning tree within a
sparse graph using limited communication links. Our first contribution is a
novel representation that enables each span to be encoded as the sum of two
positive integers, providing an optimal solution to the problem. Our
representation ensures that, given $M$ non-malicious agents, at least one
span can be decoded, while another span can be decoded if the number of
non-malicious agents falls within a specific range. We demonstrate the
effectiveness of our approach through simulations on a consensus algorithm
under the presence of malicious agents.

Using high-quality maps of the cosmic microwave background (CMB) and contemporary data from the Planck satellite, instrumental systematic effects can be recreated with high fidelity. By leveraging these realistic effects, researchers can effectively test future instruments' capabilities to make precise measurements of the CMB. This approach enables accurate simulations of future instruments, such as LiteBIRD and CMB-S4, in order to estimate their sensitivity to rare physical phenomena like gravitational waves from the early universe and to refine detection methods for a next-generation experiment. This study provides detailed instructions on implementing these effects in the CMB-S4 data analysis framework, enabling accurate estimation of the experiment's capabilities to constrain the energy of the early universe and to make precise temperature and polarization measurements of the CMB. This tool is open-source and can be utilized by researchers developing the next-generation CMB experiment to estimate the research's outcomes.

BART, a state-of-the-art model for partial tree linearization, outperforms BART on word ordering tasks, leading us to re-examine the assumptions regarding dependency trees and their relation to surface words. Our findings suggest that models may be learning fragmented trees rather than coherent structures. Furthermore, we discover that tree fragments can be reconstructed from predicted linearizations, effectively capturing the underlying information in the data. We also propose partial tree linearization as a re-framed interpretation of dependency parsing that aligns with the parsing outputs of neural sequence-to-sequence models.

Our new approach to building robust and efficient anti-spoifficacy networks combines two innovative techniques for connecting layers across different parts of a AI model. Our model, known as MDDDFAD-CX, constructs these connections in a strategic manner to improve the reliability of deepfake detection across various platforms. In the initial stage, CX connections are integrated into a basic AI model, teaching it to distinguish between real and fake data in different formats without being overwhelmed. As the model progresses, the CX connections help it to differentiate between genuine and manipulated videos, leveraging the information exchanged between different parts of the model. Our research shows that CX connections free the combination of the model from being limited to a single format, without sacrificing accuracy. Evaluations indicate that MDDDFAD-CX outperforms other advanced deepfake detection models, achieving impressive results on the DFDC benchmark, with an excellent performance record.

A. Besicovitch and A. Tartar originally defined a angle function in Euclidean spaces to determine if a space could be conformally embedded into a higher-dimensional Euclidean space. We expanded this function to apply to general metric spaces and identified specific cases where the new definition aligns with the original one. Furthermore, if a metric space can be conformally embedded into a higher-dimensional Euclidean space, our new angle function provides a limit that must be met. Conversely, if our new angle function of a space satisfies a certain condition, then that space can be conformally embedded into a higher-dimensional Euclidean space of the corresponding dimension.

We establish lower bounds for the size of the extended genus group of isomorphism classes of orders within a specific type of number field, known as a number field of rank $n$. Additionally, we determine how these lower bounds change when adjusting the conditions of integrals within their absolute value.

We investigate specific properties of a quantum group's basis, labeled as $\bar{\bf \theta}$, under operations performed by a braid group and certain automorphisms. By leveraging Jefferies' construction of the quantum group basis, $\bf U_q(\frak g)$, associated with a Lie algebra $\frak g$. Our findings on the basis $\bar{\bf \theta}$ are applied to establish the invariance of the quantum K-theiry $K_q$, as well as the quantum group $q$-polynomials, under the Lusztig actions on both the K-theiry basis and the quantum group's basis. Furthermore, we examine the behavior of the quantum group's basis $\bar{\bf \theta}$ under the Fock's isomorphism, and we provide a novel expression for the bar-inverted basis $\bar{\bf \theta}$ in terms of the Chevalley basis, achieved by applying a sequence of Lusztig's transformations. These transformations include both positive and negative components. Our results hold true for a broad class of symmetric matrices, denoted as $Q$.

A notorious characteristic of cryptocurrency is its involvement in pyramid schemes.
To assess the scale of these scams in the cryptocurrency world, our study specifically
investigates the Python protocol, which was the target of allegations of a huge
pyramid scheme.  From the Python protocol's blockchain, our researchers extracted
transaction transaction data and transaction amounts from its test network and
mainstream network.  Our examination of this data revealed that in the protocol's
20-month history, the majority of transactions occurred within the second half,
whereas the initial half saw transactions remain constant at approximately 10 per
hour.  Furthermore, our findings showed that 95% of transactions resulted in
financial losses for the participant who paid the 120-block transaction fee to
receive a return of double that amount after seven days.  From the Python protocol's
blockchain data, there is compelling evidence to support the assertion that these
cryptocurrency protocols are instrumental in enabling these pyramid schemes to
thrive.  As such, they cause considerable harm to the broader cryptocurrency
community and infringe upon the rights of the majority of the community who are
unwittingly exploited.  Due to the blockchain's immutability, the protocol's
developers cannot erase this data, which could be utilized as an invaluable
instrument for investigating and combating these scams in the future.

This investigation focuses on ten suspected globular clusters within the Milky Way, with ages between 4.0 and 12.0 billion years, utilizing high-resolution stellar models and hypershots. These "hypershots" comprehensively examine the broad range of ages, metallicity, $\mathrm{Al}/\mathrm{Na}$, and $\mathrm{Li}$ present in each cluster's stellar populations, while also taking into consideration the features of field and halo stellar populations. The suspected clusters were identified through the Gaia web tool, and their properties were determined through the process of summing the probabilities of individual stellar observations, resulting in the exclusion of open clusters and the confirmation that none of the ten clusters investigated should be classified as "retained halo star streams". The investigation signifies an important step towards a thorough analysis of all Milky Way globular clusters.
